tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# HANDOFF — take over Katalyst and carry it to a working prototype
2	
3	You are a fresh agent. You have no memory of how this project got here. This file gives you everything you need to continue. Read it fully, then read `STATUS.md` (newest entry on top), then **`PLAN.md`**.
4	
5	> **2026-09-21 — the road changed; this file's §2 and §9 describe the project before it did.** Two independent reviews were digested that day. They found three real defects in the engine's arithmetic on the demo map, and that the trade the brief ends in has no code. The road is now: finish stack 04 → **05 sound numbers, then settled shapes** → **06 the trade** → **07 a map you can argue with**. Read **`PLAN.md`** (what, in what order, the definition of done), **`design-after-midpoint-review.md`** (why), and **`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`** (what waits on Kent — nothing in stacks 05–07 is built until he answers). §4–§8 below — how Kent works, git, the environment, worktrees, the lessons — are unchanged and binding. Two working rules are new: **every whole suite, browser run and repeat bar goes through `plans/scripts/heavy.sh`, one at a time**; and **only Hormuz is recorded until Kent explicitly approves more.**
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. The mission
10	
11	Build **Katalyst**: a take-home prototype for Catalyst (catalyst.app), a seed-stage company that turns a trading idea stated in plain English into live execution.
12	
13	**What the tool does, in one sentence:** you type an event you think will happen; Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.
14	
15	The brief is `ASSIGNMENT.md`. The owner is **Kent Gang**, a solo developer. He cares most about four things, in his words: well structured with Docker and tests; proper code design; rigorously documented decisions; and a beautiful, elegant, delightful interface.
16	
17	**"Done" means:** a reviewer clones the repo, runs one command, and walks the full flow on all four example events from the brief — type a hypothesis, watch the cause-and-effect map draw itself, change a step, compare the two versions, and end on a thesis card with a derived stop-loss. Tests pass with no API key. Every number on screen can show why. Full checklist: `roadmap-03-to-06.md`, "Definition of done" (the boxes stack 03 ticked are ticked).
18	
19	---
20	
21	## 2. What is built, as of 2026-09-17 (end of stack 03)
22	
23	Stacks 01 (skeleton), 02 (schema), **03a (engine) and 03b (canvas)** are merged to `main`. Every pull request up to #27 is squash-merged (a few numbers were never used), and `main` is green on five checks.
24	
25	**The one sentence to hold on to:** *the engine computes everything and the canvas draws everything, and they have not met.* The canvas reads the stored example and shows every computed number as an absence with a reason ("no engine yet"). Joining them is the first code of stack 04.
26	
27	**Documents.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md`; `ARCHITECTURE.md` (every section says *built* or *planned*); fourteen decision records in `docs/adr/`, **0001–0014, all accepted** — next is **0015**. The spec is a book: `spec/graph/` (4 chapters), `spec/multiverse/` (4: `interventions`, `branches-and-worlds`, `propagation`, `diff`), `spec/workbench/` (6: `color-motion-type`, `tiles-ports-wires`, `layout-and-zoom`, `keyboard-and-access`, `diff-view`, `inspector`, plus the landing page's **worked example cast** and **twelve-line visual review checklist**), and `spec/vocabulary.md` with its **Interface words** table and **Words for a number that is not there**. `spec/generation/` and `spec/thesis/` are landing pages only.
28	
29	**The server** — `backend/src/katalyst/`:
30	
31	- `domain/` — the pure core, twelve files, 100% covered, `mypy --strict` clean. Models (`belief`, `proposition`, `link`, `graph`, `intervention`, `branch`, `ids`), `validity.py` (`validate` returns every fault at once; **nineteen codes**: fourteen map faults, four refused edits, one refused comparison), **`patch.py`** (`Assignment`, `apply`, `flatten`, `affected_set`, `introduced_by`), **`propagation.py`** (`World`, `Retraction`, `SeriesState`, `propagate`, `versions_of` — two thousand versions of the map × eight worlds; a supposition is a hard fact until undermined; two seed streams derived per claim), **`diff.py`** (`diff`, `DeltaRow`, `sensitivity` — `shifted` read off the paired difference; rank = size of move × weakest arrow on the best-backed route).
32	- `engine/` — `ids.py` (the only place an identifier is made) and `worlds.py` (the only place that knows a store or a date). Nothing has ever called a model.
33	- `fixtures/hormuz.py` — the worked example, now **curated**: two inputs tuned and marked **Tuned**, and every `beliefs.model` equal to its `prior` ("nothing computed yet"). Branch `br_hormuz_then_strike`.
34	- `api/` — `GET /api/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/about`, `/fixtures`, `/fixtures/{id}`, and **`POST /api/worlds`, `/api/worlds/diff`, `/api/worlds/conditional`** (a refused branch is a 422 carrying every violation). Try: `curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/worlds -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"base_id":"hormuz","seed":20261001}'`.
35	- `grounding/` — an empty package (stack 05).
36	
37	**The browser app** — `frontend/src/`: `api/schema.ts` (generated, never hand-edited) and `api/client.ts`; `world/` (the `WorldSource` seam, `FixtureWorldSource` live, **`ApiWorldSource` a stub waiting for stack 04**, hand-written `WorldView`, `branchReducer`); `graph/` (canvas, ELK layout on a background thread with pinning, `wires/` with routing and one-pass plate placement, `diff/` with the four structural states); `components/` (Tile, BeliefChip, OriginMark, Inspector, PathBar, DeltaRail, BranchPanel, Outline, CommandPalette, ShortcutsSheet, Launchpad, DirectionReadout); `keyboard/`, `a11y/`; `styles/tokens.css` (the whole visual vocabulary); `e2e/hormuz.spec.ts`.
38	
39	**Tests: 259 on the server, 177 in the browser (one skipped on purpose — it waits for the join), one keyboard-only end-to-end test.** Continuous integration: `backend`, `frontend`, `types-fresh`, `docker`, `e2e` — **no API key in any of them**.
40	
41	**What the engine says about Hormuz** (seed 20261001): *"Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck" moves [the Polymarket Brent contract] from .50 to .42 by 2026-10-04 and leaves 1 claim untouched.* A world costs about 65 ms, a difference about 200 ms.
42	
43	**Next:** stack **04**, as two parallel stacks — **04a** (browser: the join, then the map drawing itself) and **04b** (server: chapters + record 0015, the pipeline, the stream + replay, evals + ensemble + spread). Plan: `stack-04-generation.md`. **Kent answered every open question on 2026-09-17 — `plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md` — and the plan is rewritten to match. Nothing is waiting on him.**
44	
45	---
46	
47	## 3. Read these, in this order (about 50 minutes)
48	
49	1. `AGENTS.md` — the rules of the repo and the working agreements. **Binding.**
50	2. `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` — §1, §3 (eleven decisions — do not reopen them), §6.1–§6.2 (what generation must do), §7 (UX-1 to UX-14), §9 (fourteen invariants), §10 (anti-patterns), §12.
51	3. `ARCHITECTURE.md` — especially §2 (the model proposes; our code disposes) and §3 (the eight steps of a generation, with what is already built marked). **You must update it in the same pull request that makes a section real.**
52	4. `spec/README.md`, `spec/vocabulary.md`, then `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` (the feedback-arrow rule and the refusal codes), `propagation.md` B4–B7, `diff.md` (including **open question 7**), and `spec/workbench/README.md` + `diff-view.md` (the `WorldSource` seam).
53	5. `docs/adr/README.md`, then records **0006** (the model boundary — the verified API specifics), **0008**, **0012** (replay mode), **0003**, **0014**.
54	6. **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-03-round-2.md`** — eleven decisions and fourteen small ones. Binding on every later stack. Then **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md`** — six decisions and eight small ones for stack 04.
55	7. `plans/stack-04-generation.md`.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## 4. How Kent works — the rules that will get your work rejected if you break them
60	
61	**Build aggressively through milestones.** Kent's own words: *"build aggressively through milestones, I edit after the fact."* He is a co-developer, not an approver standing at a gate. Decision records and spec chapters still come first in the *stack order* — the bottom pull request of every stack is docs-only — but code above them proceeds while he reads. Nothing here is irreversible.
62	
63	**Push and open pull requests freely. Kent merges** — or asks the coordinator to, as he did for all of stack 03; then use §5. Never merge without being asked.
64	
65	**All sub-agents run on Opus.** Kent said so directly. Do not downgrade a sub-agent to save tokens.
66	
67	**Decisions come before code.** A significant architectural choice needs a decision record (`docs/adr/`, next number **0015**, copy `template.md`). Write it `proposed`, ask Kent, build only after he accepts. Small tooling choices already covered by a record need no new one.
68	
69	**How to ask him — this worked.** Collect the open questions; have a read-only Opus agent analyse them for *the most principled, simplest-to-maintain design, balanced against functionality*, sorting them into "needs Kent" and "falls out of something already decided"; then put the first group to him with the **question tool**: each in plain words with the Hormuz example, what changes on screen and in code, the recommended option first. He settled eleven questions and approved fourteen small ones in one sitting. Record the answers in a dated note under `plans/notes/` and fold them into the chapters the same day.
70	
71	**Two things Kent will veto on sight.**
72	1. **A template-looking interface.** Default component-library styling, a spinner followed by a dump of results, pop-up dialogs, a tangled hairball graph. His first reaction to the first canvas was "closer to spare than rich" — density and deliberate detail are wanted.
73	2. **Not knowing why it did that.** Any state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule, or a cited source. This applies to the product *and* to your own work: a number nobody computed is never typed by hand — not in a fixture, not in a chapter, not in a test.
74	
75	**Write plainly.** No unexplained jargon, abbreviations, or symbols; each passage stands alone; short and punchy. When you cite an invariant such as INV-4, add a few words saying what it means.
76	
77	**The spec is a book; decision records are a journal.** Do not number spec files. A journal entry's measurements are dated facts — add a dated note rather than rewriting them; a book chapter is kept true.
78	
79	**Authority stays with Kent.** Offer options with a recommendation; do not argue him into things. If you take a call on his behalf, say so, say why, and make it easy to overturn. Questions go at the bottom of `STATUS.md` under "Waiting on Kent" **and in chat**, because he does not read `plans/` unprompted.
80	
81	---
82	
83	## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)
84	
85	- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` — `feat/04a-join`, `spec/04b-generation`.
86	- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `ci:`, plus `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
87	- **Stacks:** bottom pull request targets `main`; each above targets its parent — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. **At most four deep** — which is why stack 04 is two stacks.
88	- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
89	- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.**
90	
91	### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is
92	
93	When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.
94	
95	### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)
96	
97	**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:
98	
99	```bash
100	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
101	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
102	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
103	```
104	
105	After a parent merges:
106	
107	1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
108	2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
109	   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
110	   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
111	3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
112	4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
113	5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 6. Your environment (checked 2026-09-17)
118	
119	| Tool | Version here | Note |
120	|------|--------------|------|
121	| `gh` | 2.101.0, signed in as `kgang` | Repo `kgang/katalyst`, private |
122	| `uv` | 0.12.15 | |
123	| Python | 3.12.4 | |
124	| Node | 23.3.0 locally | Docker and CI pin **24**. Use `npm ci`, not `npm install`, in a fresh worktree |
125	| Docker | 27.5.1 | |
126	| Playwright | `@playwright/test` in `frontend/` | `npx playwright install chromium` once; `npx playwright test` starts both halves itself |
127	
128	**`.env` in the main checkout is Kent's.** It is git-ignored and holds his real keys. **Never copy it into a worktree, never read it into a brief, never commit it.** `.env.example` is the one agents use.
129	
130	**Hooks:** `.claude/settings.json` runs the `entire` checkpoint tool on session events; its output on `git push` is normal. The git hooks directory has a `commit-msg` hook but **no `pre-commit` hook wired**, so the linters do not run on commit — run `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .` and `npm run lint` yourself before committing.
131	
132	**Model API key: stack 04b needs one to record cassettes and demos — and Kent must name a spending ceiling first.** Before writing *any* code that calls Claude, load the `claude-api` skill; decision record 0006 holds the verified specifics, and memory is unreliable. Continuous integration never gets a key.
133	
134	**Running the app to look at it:** backend `cd backend && env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -u FRED_API_KEY uv run uvicorn katalyst.api.main:app --port 80NN`; frontend `KATALYST_API_URL=http://localhost:80NN npm run dev -- --port 51NN --strictPort`. Give each agent its own pair of ports. For screenshots, a throwaway Playwright script **outside the repo** (the session scratchpad) at 1600 × 1000.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## 7. The worktree pattern
139	
140	Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.
141	
142	- **One agent per worktree**, except chapter writers, who may share one **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command** — the coordinator commits for them.
143	- **Disjoint owned files**, listed in the brief. "Touch nothing outside it. If something outside it must change, write why in your report."
144	- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
145	- A resumed agent (send it a message) keeps its context — use that for fix rounds and for sweeps of files it wrote. You can point a resumed agent at a *different* worktree when the fix has to land on another branch.
146	- Remove worktrees after the merge.
147	
148	---
149	
150	## 8. Lessons — read these twice
151	
152	1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
153	2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
154	3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
155	4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
156	5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
157	6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
158	7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
159	8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
160	9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
161	10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
162	11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
163	12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
164	13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
165	15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
166	16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
167	17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
168	18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
169	19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
170	20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
171	21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
172	22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost ~70 minutes that day and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
173	23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
174	14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

# HANDOFF — take over Katalyst and carry it to a working prototype

You are a fresh agent. You have no memory of how this project got here. This file gives you everything you need to continue. Read it fully, then read `STATUS.md` (newest entry on top), then **`PLAN.md`**.

> **2026-09-21 — the road changed; this file's §2 and §9 describe the project before it did.** Two independent reviews were digested that day. They found three real defects in the engine's arithmetic on the demo map, and that the trade the brief ends in has no code. The road is now: finish stack 04 → **05 sound numbers, then settled shapes** → **06 the trade** → **07 a map you can argue with**. Read **`PLAN.md`** (what, in what order, the definition of done), **`design-after-midpoint-review.md`** (why), and **`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`** (what waits on Kent — nothing in stacks 05–07 is built until he answers). §4–§8 below — how Kent works, git, the environment, worktrees, the lessons — are unchanged and binding. Two working rules are new: **every whole suite, browser run and repeat bar goes through `plans/scripts/heavy.sh`, one at a time**; and **only Hormuz is recorded until Kent explicitly approves more.**

---

## 1. The mission

Build **Katalyst**: a take-home prototype for Catalyst (catalyst.app), a seed-stage company that turns a trading idea stated in plain English into live execution.

**What the tool does, in one sentence:** you type an event you think will happen; Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.

The brief is `ASSIGNMENT.md`. The owner is **Kent Gang**, a solo developer. He cares most about four things, in his words: well structured with Docker and tests; proper code design; rigorously documented decisions; and a beautiful, elegant, delightful interface.

**"Done" means:** a reviewer clones the repo, runs one command, and walks the full flow on all four example events from the brief — type a hypothesis, watch the cause-and-effect map draw itself, change a step, compare the two versions, and end on a thesis card with a derived stop-loss. Tests pass with no API key. Every number on screen can show why. Full checklist: `roadmap-03-to-06.md`, "Definition of done" (the boxes stack 03 ticked are ticked).

---

## 2. What is built, as of 2026-09-17 (end of stack 03)

Stacks 01 (skeleton), 02 (schema), **03a (engine) and 03b (canvas)** are merged to `main`. Every pull request up to #27 is squash-merged (a few numbers were never used), and `main` is green on five checks.

**The one sentence to hold on to:** *the engine computes everything and the canvas draws everything, and they have not met.* The canvas reads the stored example and shows every computed number as an absence with a reason ("no engine yet"). Joining them is the first code of stack 04.

**Documents.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md`; `ARCHITECTURE.md` (every section says *built* or *planned*); fourteen decision records in `docs/adr/`, **0001–0014, all accepted** — next is **0015**. The spec is a book: `spec/graph/` (4 chapters), `spec/multiverse/` (4: `interventions`, `branches-and-worlds`, `propagation`, `diff`), `spec/workbench/` (6: `color-motion-type`, `tiles-ports-wires`, `layout-and-zoom`, `keyboard-and-access`, `diff-view`, `inspector`, plus the landing page's **worked example cast** and **twelve-line visual review checklist**), and `spec/vocabulary.md` with its **Interface words** table and **Words for a number that is not there**. `spec/generation/` and `spec/thesis/` are landing pages only.

**The server** — `backend/src/katalyst/`:

- `domain/` — the pure core, twelve files, 100% covered, `mypy --strict` clean. Models (`belief`, `proposition`, `link`, `graph`, `intervention`, `branch`, `ids`), `validity.py` (`validate` returns every fault at once; **nineteen codes**: fourteen map faults, four refused edits, one refused comparison), **`patch.py`** (`Assignment`, `apply`, `flatten`, `affected_set`, `introduced_by`), **`propagation.py`** (`World`, `Retraction`, `SeriesState`, `propagate`, `versions_of` — two thousand versions of the map × eight worlds; a supposition is a hard fact until undermined; two seed streams derived per claim), **`diff.py`** (`diff`, `DeltaRow`, `sensitivity` — `shifted` read off the paired difference; rank = size of move × weakest arrow on the best-backed route).
- `engine/` — `ids.py` (the only place an identifier is made) and `worlds.py` (the only place that knows a store or a date). Nothing has ever called a model.
- `fixtures/hormuz.py` — the worked example, now **curated**: two inputs tuned and marked **Tuned**, and every `beliefs.model` equal to its `prior` ("nothing computed yet"). Branch `br_hormuz_then_strike`.
- `api/` — `GET /api/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/about`, `/fixtures`, `/fixtures/{id}`, and **`POST /api/worlds`, `/api/worlds/diff`, `/api/worlds/conditional`** (a refused branch is a 422 carrying every violation). Try: `curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/worlds -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"base_id":"hormuz","seed":20261001}'`.
- `grounding/` — an empty package (stack 05).

**The browser app** — `frontend/src/`: `api/schema.ts` (generated, never hand-edited) and `api/client.ts`; `world/` (the `WorldSource` seam, `FixtureWorldSource` live, **`ApiWorldSource` a stub waiting for stack 04**, hand-written `WorldView`, `branchReducer`); `graph/` (canvas, ELK layout on a background thread with pinning, `wires/` with routing and one-pass plate placement, `diff/` with the four structural states); `components/` (Tile, BeliefChip, OriginMark, Inspector, PathBar, DeltaRail, BranchPanel, Outline, CommandPalette, ShortcutsSheet, Launchpad, DirectionReadout); `keyboard/`, `a11y/`; `styles/tokens.css` (the whole visual vocabulary); `e2e/hormuz.spec.ts`.

**Tests: 259 on the server, 177 in the browser (one skipped on purpose — it waits for the join), one keyboard-only end-to-end test.** Continuous integration: `backend`, `frontend`, `types-fresh`, `docker`, `e2e` — **no API key in any of them**.

**What the engine says about Hormuz** (seed 20261001): *"Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck" moves [the Polymarket Brent contract] from .50 to .42 by 2026-10-04 and leaves 1 claim untouched.* A world costs about 65 ms, a difference about 200 ms.

**Next:** stack **04**, as two parallel stacks — **04a** (browser: the join, then the map drawing itself) and **04b** (server: chapters + record 0015, the pipeline, the stream + replay, evals + ensemble + spread). Plan: `stack-04-generation.md`. **Kent answered every open question on 2026-09-17 — `plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md` — and the plan is rewritten to match. Nothing is waiting on him.**

---

## 3. Read these, in this order (about 50 minutes)

1. `AGENTS.md` — the rules of the repo and the working agreements. **Binding.**
2. `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` — §1, §3 (eleven decisions — do not reopen them), §6.1–§6.2 (what generation must do), §7 (UX-1 to UX-14), §9 (fourteen invariants), §10 (anti-patterns), §12.
3. `ARCHITECTURE.md` — especially §2 (the model proposes; our code disposes) and §3 (the eight steps of a generation, with what is already built marked). **You must update it in the same pull request that makes a section real.**
4. `spec/README.md`, `spec/vocabulary.md`, then `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` (the feedback-arrow rule and the refusal codes), `propagation.md` B4–B7, `diff.md` (including **open question 7**), and `spec/workbench/README.md` + `diff-view.md` (the `WorldSource` seam).
5. `docs/adr/README.md`, then records **0006** (the model boundary — the verified API specifics), **0008**, **0012** (replay mode), **0003**, **0014**.
6. **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-03-round-2.md`** — eleven decisions and fourteen small ones. Binding on every later stack. Then **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md`** — six decisions and eight small ones for stack 04.
7. `plans/stack-04-generation.md`.

---

## 4. How Kent works — the rules that will get your work rejected if you break them

**Build aggressively through milestones.** Kent's own words: *"build aggressively through milestones, I edit after the fact."* He is a co-developer, not an approver standing at a gate. Decision records and spec chapters still come first in the *stack order* — the bottom pull request of every stack is docs-only — but code above them proceeds while he reads. Nothing here is irreversible.

**Push and open pull requests freely. Kent merges** — or asks the coordinator to, as he did for all of stack 03; then use §5. Never merge without being asked.

**All sub-agents run on Opus.** Kent said so directly. Do not downgrade a sub-agent to save tokens.

**Decisions come before code.** A significant architectural choice needs a decision record (`docs/adr/`, next number **0015**, copy `template.md`). Write it `proposed`, ask Kent, build only after he accepts. Small tooling choices already covered by a record need no new one.

**How to ask him — this worked.** Collect the open questions; have a read-only Opus agent analyse them for *the most principled, simplest-to-maintain design, balanced against functionality*, sorting them into "needs Kent" and "falls out of something already decided"; then put the first group to him with the **question tool**: each in plain words with the Hormuz example, what changes on screen and in code, the recommended option first. He settled eleven questions and approved fourteen small ones in one sitting. Record the answers in a dated note under `plans/notes/` and fold them into the chapters the same day.

**Two things Kent will veto on sight.**
1. **A template-looking interface.** Default component-library styling, a spinner followed by a dump of results, pop-up dialogs, a tangled hairball graph. His first reaction to the first canvas was "closer to spare than rich" — density and deliberate detail are wanted.
2. **Not knowing why it did that.** Any state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule, or a cited source. This applies to the product *and* to your own work: a number nobody computed is never typed by hand — not in a fixture, not in a chapter, not in a test.

**Write plainly.** No unexplained jargon, abbreviations, or symbols; each passage stands alone; short and punchy. When you cite an invariant such as INV-4, add a few words saying what it means.

**The spec is a book; decision records are a journal.** Do not number spec files. A journal entry's measurements are dated facts — add a dated note rather than rewriting them; a book chapter is kept true.

**Authority stays with Kent.** Offer options with a recommendation; do not argue him into things. If you take a call on his behalf, say so, say why, and make it easy to overturn. Questions go at the bottom of `STATUS.md` under "Waiting on Kent" **and in chat**, because he does not read `plans/` unprompted.

---

## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)

- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` — `feat/04a-join`, `spec/04b-generation`.
- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `ci:`, plus `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
- **Stacks:** bottom pull request targets `main`; each above targets its parent — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. **At most four deep** — which is why stack 04 is two stacks.
- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.**

### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is

When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.

### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)

**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:

```bash
gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
```

After a parent merges:

1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.

---

## 6. Your environment (checked 2026-09-17)

| Tool | Version here | Note |
|------|--------------|------|
| `gh` | 2.101.0, signed in as `kgang` | Repo `kgang/katalyst`, private |
| `uv` | 0.12.15 | |
| Python | 3.12.4 | |
| Node | 23.3.0 locally | Docker and CI pin **24**. Use `npm ci`, not `npm install`, in a fresh worktree |
| Docker | 27.5.1 | |
| Playwright | `@playwright/test` in `frontend/` | `npx playwright install chromium` once; `npx playwright test` starts both halves itself |

**`.env` in the main checkout is Kent's.** It is git-ignored and holds his real keys. **Never copy it into a worktree, never read it into a brief, never commit it.** `.env.example` is the one agents use.

**Hooks:** `.claude/settings.json` runs the `entire` checkpoint tool on session events; its output on `git push` is normal. The git hooks directory has a `commit-msg` hook but **no `pre-commit` hook wired**, so the linters do not run on commit — run `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .` and `npm run lint` yourself before committing.

**Model API key: stack 04b needs one to record cassettes and demos — and Kent must name a spending ceiling first.** Before writing *any* code that calls Claude, load the `claude-api` skill; decision record 0006 holds the verified specifics, and memory is unreliable. Continuous integration never gets a key.

**Running the app to look at it:** backend `cd backend && env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -u FRED_API_KEY uv run uvicorn katalyst.api.main:app --port 80NN`; frontend `KATALYST_API_URL=http://localhost:80NN npm run dev -- --port 51NN --strictPort`. Give each agent its own pair of ports. For screenshots, a throwaway Playwright script **outside the repo** (the session scratchpad) at 1600 × 1000.

---

## 7. The worktree pattern

Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.

- **One agent per worktree**, except chapter writers, who may share one **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command** — the coordinator commits for them.
- **Disjoint owned files**, listed in the brief. "Touch nothing outside it. If something outside it must change, write why in your report."
- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
- A resumed agent (send it a message) keeps its context — use that for fix rounds and for sweeps of files it wrote. You can point a resumed agent at a *different* worktree when the fix has to land on another branch.
- Remove worktrees after the merge.

---

## 8. Lessons — read these twice

1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost ~70 minutes that day and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

---

## 9. The road from here

| Stack | What it proves | Plan |
|-------|----------------|------|
| ~~01 skeleton~~ · ~~02 schema~~ | **Merged.** | history |
| ~~03a engine ∥ 03b canvas~~ | **Merged 2026-09-17.** Changing one step re-computes only what is downstream; the map is dense, readable and keyboard-driven | `stack-03a-engine.md`, `stack-03b-canvas.md` (history) |
| **04a join + growth ∥ 04b generation** | **Next.** The canvas shows the engine's numbers; the model draws a real map for any hypothesis, streamed step by step; with no key the four examples replay | `stack-04-generation.md` |
| 05 thesis | The map compiles to a trade with a derived stop-loss and live market prices | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
| 06 probes | Extra modeling effort where the user points it (stretch) | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
| 07 presentable (proposed) | README walkthrough, a pastcast self-test, a last accessibility sweep | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |

**This table is history as of 2026-09-21. Start with `PLAN.md`** — stacks 05, 06 and 07 mean different things now, and several of their lines wait on Kent (`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`).

export KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT=${KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT:-8079}

# run into one render, and generate.spec.ts's subject is a map *arriving*: with

unset KATALYST_REPLAY_INSTANT

# The first two minutes

## What

Nine things a reviewer meets before they have decided anything. No domain change, no schema change, no new concept — one browser branch off the growing map.

**A mouse can reach the thing this product is for.** The panel of operations had exactly two ways in: the `E` key and a command in the palette. Somebody working the screen by pointing at things could click every tile, read the whole argument, find no verb anywhere on it and conclude the tool is a viewer. The Inspector's head now carries the way in — **Change this claim** on a claim, **Change this push** on an arrow — in the vocabulary's own words, as a word with a hairline round it. It is in the panel's head rather than on the tile because a tile's height is reserved before the browser has drawn one, so a new row on a tile lays the whole map out again. It is handed over only while the operations are shut: a way in that is already in is not a control, and on an arrow a second one would put two buttons reading *Change this push* on one screen.

**The two operations that are easiest to confuse say the difference before the press.** *Suppose this is true* and *This happened* both fix a claim's value and differ in what else may move. That was spoken only after the click, by which time the reader has chosen. Each now carries the shared vocabulary's own meaning as a subtitle, word for word from the *Interface words* table.

**Nothing on the panel takes a press and then explains that it cannot act.** *Split this claim · not yet built* is gone until it is built. Its words stay settled in the vocabulary and what it would do stays written in the interventions chapter.

**The change list leads with its rows.** The heading used to be followed by a four-or-five-line summary and a three-line methodology note: seven lines of prose between a reader and the one artefact that answers *what did my edit do, ranked*. The rows come first, the note is the caption it already read like, and the summary closes. Ranked against unranked, the *no change* row and the reason line are untouched.

**The map read as a list is one sentence wide again.** An outline item was a two-column grid, `2.4em 1fr`, whose first column held a claim letter that was taken off every surface when identifiers stopped being printed. The track stayed, and a grid puts its one remaining child in the first track — so every sentence was wrapping inside two and a half characters. One column now, floored at zero.

**Two rules that said the opposite of the rule in force are deleted.** `.branch-panel`'s `max-height: 28%` and `overflow-y: auto`, and `.intervene`'s `overflow-y: auto`. `.page--map .dock > *` is two classes to their one and already won with `max-height: none; overflow: visible`.

**The first screen offers only what this copy can do.** Only the Strait of Hormuz is recorded, so with no key three of the four cards read *not yet live* and the four of them took the whole right-hand column. A card is now only ever something a reader can take up; what is left of the rest is the line that was already under them, naming which examples they were. **Six states, each saying a different true thing** — the readiness ask in flight; the readiness ask that did not come back; a key configured; no key with a recording; no key without one; and nothing recorded at all — and the two that look alike are two on purpose, because a question in flight invites waiting and an ask that got no reply invites asking again. Collapsing those two was a real defect: a failed `/api/readyz` left the screen saying *asking the server* for ever. At the foot, the **model key** row stays a labelled row and `server` and `version` fold into one quiet line beneath it.

**And the way in does not drop the keyboard.** *Change this claim* unmounts the moment it is pressed, so tabbing to it and pressing Enter would have left a reader standing on nothing. The panel takes the keyboard when it opens — the reader's own act, and `graph/theKeyboard.ts`'s rule is about who decided — and the screen puts it back where it came from when the panel closes, or on the control that has replaced it where that is gone.

**The tile's movement line says which day it is read on.** One claim carried two pairs of numbers — the tile reads it on its judging day, the change list reads each row on the day the two maps are furthest apart — and a reviewer who notices concludes one is wrong. The clause is on the hover and in the accessible description rather than in the drawn words, because the drawn words are what reserve the tile's height and the clause takes the line to two lines in some states and not others.

**And a browser check that would have caught every layout defect the interface audit found.** At 1600 × 1000, 1440 × 900 and 1280 × 800, with a branch open and the operations open, three questions of every button, link and field in the panel: it is drawn at a size; scrolled to, it lies inside the part of the panel that is on the glass; and **at its own centre the topmost thing on the screen is that control** — the overlap test, and the one that catches a sibling drawn over a button. Plus one assertion that varies with the window, since the panel is a fixed 336 pixels: the page never scrolls sideways. Plus the mouse journey above, end to end, with no key pressed. Plus `trace: "retain-on-failure"` and an upload step, because two failures were lost last week with a line of output and nothing else.

**The check found its first defect before it was ever run.** The three likelihood fields of *My own number* sat in `repeat(3, 1fr)` with no floor — three inputs whose min-content width is about 140 pixels each, in a 303-pixel column — so they ran past the panel's right edge. `minmax(0, 1fr)` and `min-width: 0`, which is the guard every other multi-track grid here already carries.

## Which invariant it satisfies

- **INV-workbench.74 — nothing is silently inert without a key.** Amended rather than merely obeyed: a launchpad card with no key *and* no recording satisfies it by not being drawn, and *Split this claim* by not being offered. A control a reader counted and cannot use is the same fault as one that does nothing when pressed.
- **The traceability veto** (`AGENTS.md`, working agreements): the first screen no longer reads *no model key* before the server has said anything, and the tile's movement line no longer leaves two readings of one claim with only one of them dated.
- **INV-12 and the colour law** are untouched, and the three architectural tests that guard them — `notByColourAlone`, `colourLaw`, `motionBudget` — stay green. Every new control is a word with a hairline round it; no new colour, no dialog, no spinner, no default component styling.
- **The diff view's promise that nothing already placed moves.** `roomFor` and every reserved tile height are unchanged, and a test says so: the new clause is in the hover precisely because the drawn line cannot grow.
- **The visual review checklist** in `spec/workbench/README.md`: the second half of the line about nothing being hidden behind anything — no control in the panel — and the readability of the list, are now checked by a machine at three windows, geometrically and never by a stored picture. The chapter says exactly that much and no more: the map's own overlaps, the template, greyscale, contrast and the eight-pixel grid still need a person and a picture.

## What is deliberately not here

- **`36%` instead of `.36`.** It goes with the refactor that moves number formatting out of the pure rules layer; done alone it re-sweeps every number in the spec in the same week the numbers are being inventoried.
- **Guess before reveal**, and **Release / undo-this-edit** — the second needs a domain change, not a browser one.
- **The *Run details* section**: the origin strip's routes, seed and loop counts stay where they are until the dock work they share lands.
- **Collapsing the tile's empty belief columns**, which is what makes room for the distribution strip and belongs with it.
- **The greyed *versions disagree* row and the *no change* sentence reading the engine's new word**: both need a schema field arriving on another branch.
- **A stored screenshot assertion.** A pixel baseline over a canvas with a background-threaded layout engine, two variable fonts and an arrival animation fails for reasons that are not faults. The geometric assertion catches the same defects and cannot flake on a font hint.

5	//
6	//   APP=http://localhost:5183 OUT=/abs/dir node /abs/path/polish-look.mjs
7	//
8	// Writes PNGs and one findings.json (focus checks, overflow checks, titles).

10	import { createRequire } from "node:module";
11	import { mkdirSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
12	
13	const require = createRequire(`${process.cwd()}/`);
14	const { chromium } = require("@playwright/test");
15	
16	const APP = process.env.APP ?? "http://localhost:5183";
17	const OUT = process.env.OUT ?? `${process.cwd()}/polish-look`;
18	mkdirSync(OUT, { recursive: true });
19	
20	const WINDOWS = [
21	  { width: 1600, height: 1000 },
22	  { width: 1440, height: 900 },
23	  { width: 1280, height: 800 },
24	];
25	const findings = {};
26	
27	async function laidOut(page, tiles) {
28	  await page.waitForFunction(
29	    (n) => {
30	      const nodes = [...document.querySelectorAll(".react-flow__node")];
31	      return nodes.length === n && new Set(nodes.map((x) => x.style.transform)).size === n;
32	    },
33	    tiles,
34	    { timeout: 30_000 },
35	  );
36	  await page.waitForTimeout(900); // the framing animation
37	}
38	
39	async function insidePanel(page, selector) {
40	  // Every matching control: is its box inside the dock's box, left to right?
41	  return page.evaluate((sel) => {
42	    const dock = document.querySelector(".dock")?.getBoundingClientRect();
43	    if (!dock) return { error: "no .dock" };
44	    return [...document.querySelectorAll(sel)].map((el) => {
45	      const r = el.getBoundingClientRect();
46	      return {
47	        label: el.getAttribute("aria-label") ?? el.id ?? el.name ?? el.tagName,
48	        left: Math.round(r.left),
49	        right: Math.round(r.right),
50	        dockRight: Math.round(dock.right),
51	        inside: r.left >= dock.left - 0.5 && r.right <= dock.right + 0.5,
52	      };
53	    });
54	  }, selector);
55	}
56	
57	const browser = await chromium.launch();
58	for (const w of WINDOWS) {
59	  const tag = `${w.width}x${w.height}`;
60	  const f = (findings[tag] = {});
61	  if (!process.env.ONLY_GONE) await theWalk(w, tag, f);
62	  await serverGone(w, tag, f);
63	}
64	await browser.close();
65	writeFileSync(`${OUT}/findings${process.env.ONLY_GONE ? "-server-gone" : ""}.json`, JSON.stringify(findings, null, 2));
66	console.log(`wrote ${OUT}`);
67	
68	async function theWalk(w, tag, f) {
69	  const context = await browser.newContext({ viewport: w, deviceScaleFactor: 2 });
70	  const page = await context.newPage();
71	  const shot = (name) => page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/${tag}-${name}.png` });
72	
73	  // 1 · the launchpad, one recording, no key
74	  await page.goto(APP);
75	  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /Strait of Hormuz/ }).first().waitFor();
76	  await page.waitForTimeout(600);
77	  await shot("01-launchpad");
78	
79	  // 2 · the map, a claim chosen with the mouse: the way in, in the Inspector's head
80	  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /Strait of Hormuz/ }).first().click();
81	  await laidOut(page, 7);
82	  await page.locator('.react-flow__node[data-id="B"]').click();
83	  const wayIn = page.getByRole("button", { name: "Change this claim" });
84	  await wayIn.waitFor();
85	  await shot("02-inspector-way-in");
86	  await page.locator(".dock").screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/${tag}-02b-dock-only.png` });
87	
88	  // 3 · focus: Tab to the way in, Enter — where is the keyboard? Then Done.
89	  await wayIn.focus();
90	  await page.keyboard.press("Enter");
91	  await page.locator('.intervene[data-about="B"]').waitFor();
92	  await page.waitForTimeout(200);
93	  f.focusAfterOpen = await page.evaluate(() => {
94	    const a = document.activeElement;
95	    return {
96	      tag: a?.tagName,
97	      text: (a?.textContent ?? "").trim().slice(0, 60),
98	      insideOperations: !!a?.closest(".intervene"),
99	    };
100	  });
101	  await page.keyboard.press("Tab");
102	  f.focusAfterOneTab = await page.evaluate(() => {
103	    const a = document.activeElement;
104	    return {
105	      tag: a?.tagName,
106	      text: (a?.textContent ?? "").trim().slice(0, 60),
107	      insideOperations: !!a?.closest(".intervene"),
108	    };
109	  });
110	  await shot("03-operations-open");
111	  await page.locator(".dock").screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/${tag}-03b-dock-only.png` });
112	  f.operationsOffered = await page
113	    .locator(".intervene button")
114	    .evaluateAll((bs) => bs.map((b) => (b.textContent ?? "").trim().slice(0, 90)));
115	
116	  // 4 · My own number: three fields inside the panel's right edge
117	  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /^My own number/ }).click();
118	  await page.getByLabel(/Your likelihood/).waitFor();
119	  await page.waitForTimeout(200);
120	  f.myOwnNumberFields = await insidePanel(page, ".intervene input");
121	  f.pageScrollsSideways = await page.evaluate(
122	    () => document.documentElement.scrollWidth > document.documentElement.clientWidth,
123	  );
124	  await shot("04-my-own-number");
125	  await page.locator(".dock").screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/${tag}-04b-dock-only.png` });
126	
127	  // Done returns the keyboard
128	  const done = page.locator(".intervene").getByRole("button", { name: /^Done/ });
129	  if (await done.count()) {
130	    await done.first().click();
131	    await page.waitForTimeout(200);
132	    f.focusAfterDone = await page.evaluate(() => {
133	      const a = document.activeElement;
134	      return { tag: a?.tagName, text: (a?.textContent ?? "").trim().slice(0, 60) };
135	    });
136	  } else {
137	    f.focusAfterDone = "no Done button found";
138	  }
139	
140	  // 5 · the strike branch: the change list leads with its rows
141	  await page.keyboard.press("Meta+k");
142	  await page.getByText(/Every command, by name/).waitFor();
143	  await shot("05a-palette");
144	  await page.keyboard.type("Hormuz opens");
145	  await page.keyboard.press("Enter");
146	  await page.locator(".map-live", { hasText: "Branch created." }).waitFor({ timeout: 30_000 });
147	  await laidOut(page, 8);

149	  await page.locator(".dock").screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/${tag}-05b-dock-only.png` });
150	  f.liveSentence = await page.locator(".map-live").textContent();
151	  f.tileTitles = await page
152	    .locator(".react-flow__node [title]")
153	    .evaluateAll((els) => els.map((e) => e.getAttribute("title")).filter((t) => t && t.length > 20));
154	
155	  // 6 · greyscale of the same screen
156	  await page.addStyleTag({ content: "html{filter:grayscale(1)!important}" }).then(async (h) => {
157	    await page.waitForTimeout(150);
158	    await shot("06-strike-branch-grey");

161	
162	  // 7 · the outline: a sentence wide

164	  await page.keyboard.press("O");
165	  await page.getByRole("tree").waitFor();
166	  await page.waitForTimeout(300);
167	  await shot("07-outline");
168	  await page.locator(".dock").screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/${tag}-07b-dock-only.png` });
169	  f.outlineItemWidths = await page
170	    .locator('[role="treeitem"]')
171	    .evaluateAll((els) => els.slice(0, 8).map((e) => Math.round(e.getBoundingClientRect().width)));
172	
173	  await context.close();
174	}

176	async function serverGone(w, tag, f) {
177	  // 8 · the launchpad when the readiness ask never comes back
178	  const dead = await browser.newContext({ viewport: w, deviceScaleFactor: 2 });
